world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Turunen, Aimo 1946, 1950. Lyydiläismurteiden äännehistoria (Ludian historical phonology). Not online; Pahomov 2017 thesis (read, helda.helsinki.fi) presupposes fixed initial main stress but states no rule.

new_statements.quote: Word stress in Karelian is constant. The primary stress always falls on the first syllable (pái-men / pái-moi 'a shepherd'), with the exception of some late Russian borrowings, in which the primary stress may sometimes fall on other syllables. [...] The Karelian language always features secondary stress, which usually falls on every odd syllable of a compound noun, excluding the last one, while the second and even syllables remain unstressed [...] In dialects with apocope, syllables with primary and secondary stress have moved closer to one another, which results in the last syllable retaining a secondary stress (Ludic: méč-ník / méč-ník-ke).
new_statements.citation: Novak, Irina; Penttonen, Martti; Ruuskanen, Aleksi; Siilin, Lea. 2022. Karelian in Grammars: A study of phonetic and morphological variation. Scientific electronic edition. Petrozavodsk: KarRC RAS. ISBN 978-5-9274-0934-1. (English ed. of Karel'skij jazyk v grammatikah, 2019.)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary word stress is fixed on the first syllable of the word in all Karelian varieties including Ludic; only some recent Russian loans may keep non-initial stress (and loans are normally adapted by moving stress to the first syllable, e.g. sámovuara < samovár).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on every odd-numbered syllable except the last; primary and secondary never adjacent; in apocopating dialects such as Ludic the (now) final syllable can retain secondary stress (méč-ník < méč-ník-ke); in compounds secondary stress on the first syllable of the second member.
new_statements.exceptions: Some late Russian borrowings may carry primary stress on a non-initial syllable; in connected speech stress may be lost or shift.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level statement for content words ('every content word has stress'); dynamic stress without vowel reduction; statement is made for Karelian as a whole (Karelian Proper, Livvi, Ludic) with a Ludic-specific example, synthesized from 21 grammars incl. three Ludic ones (Genetz 1872, Barantsev 1985 ms., Virtaranta 1986) and citing Barantsev 1975: 197.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statement is made for 'Karelian' in the Russian/KarRC sense, which treats Ludic (ludi1246) as one of three main dialects alongside Karelian Proper (kare1335) and Livvi (livv1243); the chapter gives a Ludic-specific example (méč-ník) and cites Barantsev 1975: 197 (Svyatozero = South Ludic). The Ludic grammars underlying the study are Genetz 1872 (North/Central Ludic), Barantsev 1985 ms. (Svyatozero, South Ludic) and Virtaranta 1986 (Haljärvi, North Ludic). Mikhailovskoye (Kuujärvi) Ludic is treated as a Ludic subdialect in the same work.

sources.locator: Ch. 6 'Word stress', p. 81 (Phonetics and phonology part)
sources.note: Ch. 6 'Word stress', p. 81: Karelian (Karelian Proper, Livvi, Ludic) has dynamic, constant word stress; primary stress always on the first syllable except some late Russian loans; secondary stress on odd non-final syllables; in apocopating dialects the final syllable may keep secondary stress (Ludic example méč-ník / méč-ník-ke); compounds: primary on first syllable of first member, secondary on first syllable of second member. Cites Barantsev 1975: 197 among others.
